routes.description: Establish that objective evaluative facts are required to account for rational assessment and that moral appearances can provide defeasible justification without first earning support through best-explanation reasoning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supports objective moral facts against desire-based and projectivist alternatives, establishes a defensible appearance-based source of prima facie justification, and connects that epistemology to basic moral knowledge.

motionBridge.description: Connect the case for irreducible evaluative facts with a route from moral appearances to justified moral belief and knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Show that rationally assessing desires, actions, and suffering requires truth-valued evaluative standards rather than attitudes alone.
Establish that appearances confer defeasible prima facie justification and are epistemically prior to explanatory inference.
Show that understanding evaluative and experiential subject matter can justify elementary moral judgments as instances of a priori knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how evaluative judgments can shape desires, emotions, and conduct rather than merely projecting antecedent attitudes.
Identify necessary judgments that resist reduction to linguistic or conceptual analyticity and thereby support broader rationalism.

routes.description: Establish that normative reasons depend on an agent's desires and deliberative standpoint, while moral belief lacks justification because objective moral facts are unnecessary in the best explanation of moral experience.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it accounts for reasons and moralized conduct without objective value, defends an explanatory standard for evidence, and shows that moral facts neither ground categorical reasons nor contribute indispensable explanatory work.

motionBridge.description: Connect the denial of attitude-independent value with the claim that moral belief lacks the evidence required for moral knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Ground normative reasons in desires, goals, values, or an agent's deliberative perspective rather than categorical demands.
Require justified belief to arise from causally informed explanatory support and show that moral facts are evidentially idle.
Explain the acquisition of concepts and causal models without presupposing contentful appearances accepted as initially true.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for moral judgment and continued moralized conduct through projected values, emotions, and stable concerns.
Interpret mathematical and modal reflection through conceptual application, experiential relations, or a broadened account of analyticity.

sections.title: Objective Value and the Error-Theoretic Burden
sections.rationale: This issue frames the motion-level dispute over whether elementary moral judgments track attitude-independent facts or whether value is exhausted by human attitudes and practices.

sections.title: Desires, Reasons, and Rational Authority
sections.rationale: The existence of categorical reasons is the principal metaphysical pathway between theories of agency and the existence or nonexistence of objective moral obligations.

sections.title: Appearances, Explanation, and Epistemic Foundations
sections.rationale: This issue directly determines whether moral appearances may justify belief prima facie or whether evidence requires causal and best-explanation support that leaves moral facts idle.

sections.title: Moral Belief, Emotion, and Projection
sections.rationale: The causal relationship among judgment, desire, emotion, and conduct bears on whether moral thought responds to facts or projects antecedent evaluative attitudes.

sections.title: A Priori Knowledge, Concepts, and Analyticity
sections.rationale: The scope of a priori justification tests whether reflection can disclose substantive truths about suffering and badness or only relations internal to concepts and their application.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: Error theory is less initially plausible than elementary moral judgments that suffering is bad and torturing people for fun is wrong.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: Appearances confer defeasible prima facie justification, because denying all appearance-based justification would leave the denial itself unjustified.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Desires alone cannot explain rational action because deciding which present, future, or imagined desires to follow requires evaluative assessment.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Centrality to self-conception does not by itself confer rational authority, since weakness of will and arbitrary higher-order desires can occur without a principled hierarchy.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: Abandoning belief in objective moral facts would substantially alter many people's desires, emotions, charitable conduct, and interpretation of ordinary actions.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-08.proposition: Intellectual moral judgments can override stronger emotional attractions, while beliefs about justice can shape the emotions that motivate intervention.

chunk-003:c003-04.proposition: Causal and best-explanation reasoning cannot begin unless agents initially accept that things are generally as they appear to be.

chunk-003:c003-08.proposition: Necessary a priori truths such as the incompatibility of being wholly red and wholly blue appear synthetic because synonym substitution does not reduce them to logical truths.

chunk-003:c003-10.proposition: A priori knowledge concerns the natures of things rather than merely words or concepts, so understanding suffering and badness can justify the judgment that suffering is bad.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Objective moral facts do not exist because valuing reflects human attitudes and practices rather than attitude-independent standards ratified by the universe.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Moral obligations would require desire-independent categorical reasons, but intelligible reasons arise from promoting desires, so such moral obligations do not exist.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Evidence supports belief when the belief's truth best explains experience, but moral truths do not best explain moral experience and therefore cannot ground moral knowledge.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: If moral facts entail desire-independent reasons and all reasons depend on desires, then there are no moral facts; evaluating the disputed premise requires comparing the rival worldviews.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: Overpowering desires do not refute a desire-based theory because normative weight tracks a desire's centrality to the agent's self-conception rather than its momentary motivational force.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: Moral belief projects antecedent values onto the world, so abandoning belief in objective morality would ordinarily leave the underlying attitudes and conduct intact.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-09.proposition: Emotions generally cause moral judgments, while apparently unemotional deliberation can still express stable cold passions connected to an agent's self-conception.

chunk-003:c003-03.proposition: Experience supports belief through background causal understanding, not because experience possesses propositional content that directly confers prima facie justification.

chunk-003:c003-07.proposition: Mathematical reflection supplies experiential evidence about correct conceptual application and relations rather than justification through intellectual seemings whose content is a mathematical proposition.

chunk-003:c003-09.proposition: The incompatibility of being wholly red and wholly blue is analytic in a broad sense because grasping the phenomenal concepts manifests understanding that their joint application is inconsistent.
